title: What an Old Testament Theocracy Actually Was
subtitle: A people God ruled directly, a moment that pointed past itself, and why no one can build it again.

sections.title: A Covenant, Not a Constitution
sections.body:
We reach for the word theocracy as if it described a kind of government, the way monarchy or republic does. It does not. The word means the rule of God, and when ancient Israel stood at the foot of Sinai it meant something closer to a marriage than a parliament. The people had been carried out of Egypt on no merit of their own. Then a voice on the mountain did not hand them a system of administration. It made a covenant. 'You shall be my treasured possession among all peoples,' the Lord said in Exodus 19, 'and you shall be to me a kingdom of priests and a holy nation.' That is the founding sentence, and it is not constitutional language. It is the language of belonging.

This is the first thing the modern reader, dreaming of a biblical government, has to feel in the chest before anything else makes sense. Israel was not a nation that happened to be religious. Israel was a people brought into existence by a relationship, and the relationship came first. The law that followed, all of it, was the shape that relationship took in fields and courtrooms and kitchens. Meredith Kline spent his life showing that the Sinai covenant was patterned on the treaty forms of the ancient Near East, where a great king bound a people to himself, named what he had done for them, and then named how they would live. The law was never the foundation. The law was the answer to a rescue already accomplished.

So to ask 'what was the structure of the theocracy' is already to ask a slightly wrong question, the way asking for the bylaws of a friendship would be wrong. There were structures. There were judges and elders and priests and, eventually, kings. But none of them sat at the center. The center was a God who had said, in effect, you are mine, and I will dwell among you. The tabernacle in the middle of the camp was the whole point made visible. The Ruler did not live in a palace at the edge. He lived in a tent in the center, and the tribes arranged themselves around his presence.

sections.title: Three Kinds of Law, One Covenant
sections.body:
When Christians have tried to read Israel's law honestly, they have long noticed that it does not all function the same way. Some commands describe how a human being ought to treat God and neighbor in any place and any century. Do not murder. Do not bear false witness. Honor your father and mother. Other commands govern the running of one specific nation in one specific land, with its own courts, its own property law, its own penalties for theft and assault. Still other commands order the worship of that nation, its sacrifices, its festivals, its clean and unclean, the whole machinery of the tabernacle and later the temple. Thomas Aquinas set this out in the Summa Theologiae, dividing the law of Moses into the moral, the judicial or civil, and the ceremonial, and the Westminster Confession carried the same threefold division into the Reformed tradition in its nineteenth chapter.

The distinction is a tool, not a fence God drew in the text, and careful readers have always known that the lines blur. Christopher Wright has cautioned against treating the three categories as neat boxes, because a single law can carry moral weight, civil function, and ceremonial meaning all at once. The Sabbath is moral rest, civil legislation, and a sign pointing to a deeper rest, all in one command. Still the distinction earns its keep. It explains why a Christian feels rightly bound by 'do not steal' and rightly unbound from the law about goring oxen or the prohibition on mixing fabrics. The first speaks the unchanging will of God. The second governed a society that no longer exists. The third pointed forward to a fulfillment that has come.

This matters enormously for anyone imagining a biblical government, because the dream usually involves lifting Israel's civil code straight off the page and dropping it into a modern state. But the civil law was the constitution of a particular people on a particular strip of land under a particular covenant. To say the moral law endures is not to say the civil penalties endure. The genius of Israel's law was never the penalties. It was the vision of a whole society ordered toward God and bent toward the poor, the widow, the stranger at the gate. That vision still indicts us. The statute book that delivered it belonged to a world that has passed.

sections.title: No King, Then a King
sections.body:
For a long stretch Israel had no king at all, and that was the design. The book of Judges describes a loose confederation of tribes with no standing government, raised up by occasional leaders when crisis came and then settling back into the rule of God through covenant, elders, and priests. It was not tidy. Judges ends with the bleak refrain that everyone did what was right in his own eyes. But the absence of a throne was not an oversight. It was a claim. The Lord was king, and Gideon said so plainly when the people begged him to rule over them. 'I will not rule over you,' he answered, 'the Lord will rule over you.'

Then in 1 Samuel 8 the people came to the old prophet and asked for a king, to be like the other nations. And God gave Samuel a strange instruction. Warn them, he said, but give them what they ask. So Samuel told them exactly what a king would cost, and the speech is one of the most clear-eyed descriptions of state power in any ancient text. He will take your sons for his armies and your daughters for his kitchens, the best of your fields and your vineyards for his servants, a tenth of your grain and a tenth of your flocks for his table. The verb tolls through the passage like a bell. He will take, and take, and take, and in the end, Samuel says, you yourselves will be his slaves.

The monarchy, then, was a concession, granted in the same breath as a warning. This is not a small detail for someone who imagines that Scripture endorses a strong religious government. The clearest biblical statement about centralized power, delivered by God's own prophet, is a warning that such power consumes the very people it claims to serve. God permitted the king. He even worked through the line of David toward the Messiah. But he never pretended the throne was the original design, and he never let Israel forget that the day they chose a man to rule them was a day they had, in part, rejected him.

sections.title: The Prophets as the Check
sections.body:
Every government accumulates power and then protects it. Israel's covenant built in a counterweight unlike anything in the surrounding empires. The prophet stood outside the palace and answered to no king, and his whole vocation was to speak the word of God against the powerful when they broke covenant. In Egypt or Babylon the king was a god or the son of one, and no one corrected him. In Israel a shepherd or a farmer could walk into the throne room and tell the king he had sinned, and the king, if he feared the Lord, had to listen.

Nathan walked in to David, the greatest of the kings, after David had stolen a man's wife and arranged his death, and told him a story about a rich man who took a poor man's only lamb. When David burned with anger at the rich man, Nathan said four words that no court prophet in any other ancient nation would have survived saying. 'You are the man.' Elijah confronted Ahab. Amos thundered against the merchants of the north who sold the righteous for silver and the needy for a pair of sandals, who trampled the head of the poor into the dust. The prophets were not chaplains blessing the regime. They were the regime's appointed accusers.

This is the wisdom that should stop anyone who romanticizes the theocracy into a tidy union of throne and altar. The actual covenant kept throne and altar in tension on purpose. The system assumed that power would corrupt, and it placed a permanent, divinely authorized voice of protest where the king could not silence it without indicting himself before God. We did not invent the idea that authority must answer to a higher law. Israel lived it, badly and unevenly, three thousand years ago, and the prophets paid for it with their freedom and sometimes their lives.

sections.title: The Parts We Find Strange
sections.body:
An honest account cannot skip the pages that trouble the modern reader, because pretending they are not there is its own kind of failure. There is the herem, the command in the conquest of Canaan to devote whole cities to destruction. There is the holiness code, with its death penalties and its long lists of what makes a body clean or unclean. There is the entire ceremonial apparatus, the blood and the smoke and the careful gradations of sacred space. To a person raised on modern sensibilities these read as primitive at best and monstrous at worst, and the discomfort is not something faith should rush to soothe away.

Two things have to be held together. The first is that these belonged to that moment in a way they belong to no other. The herem was a singular, bounded act of judgment on specific peoples whose cup of iniquity, in the language of Genesis 15, had filled up, carried out in one generation under direct divine command and never offered as a pattern for any nation afterward. The holiness laws drew a hard line around a people meant to be set apart, surrounded by cultures that practiced child sacrifice and temple prostitution, and the severity was the severity of a people being kept distinct so that something could come through them. The ceremonial system taught a whole nation, in the only language an ancient people could read, that sin is real, that it kills, that approaching a holy God costs blood.

The second thing is that all of it pointed past itself. The book of Hebrews reads the entire sacrificial system as a shadow cast backward by a reality not yet arrived. The blood of bulls and goats could never take away sins. It was a long, repeated, deliberately incomplete rehearsal for the one sacrifice that would. The strange parts were strange because they were temporary, a scaffold raised around a building under construction. When the building stood, the scaffold came down. We do not keep the scaffold or defend it as though it were the house. We read it as the thing that held the shape until the true thing came, and the true thing was a person.

sections.title: Why It Cannot Be Rebuilt
sections.body:
Here is the conclusion the whole argument has been moving toward. The theocracy cannot be rebuilt, and the attempt to rebuild it misreads the entire shape of the story. Israel was a unique people, in a unique land, under a unique covenant, and every part of that uniqueness was bent toward one purpose. To bring the Messiah into the world. The land and the bloodline were not real estate and genealogy. The whole arrangement was the riverbed through which a single life would one day flow, and once that life arrived, the riverbed had done its work.

Before answering it, the position deserves to be stated at full strength, by the men who argued it best. Greg Bahnsen, in his 1977 Theonomy in Christian Ethics, and R.J. Rushdoony, in his 1973 Institutes of Biblical Law, did not build a case out of bigotry or laziness. They built it out of two convictions that are difficult to refute. The first is that God's law is good, that the statutes given at Sinai express the will of a holy God and not the passing taste of a Bronze Age tribe, so that what God once called just cannot have become unjust. The second is that no society is neutral, that every legal order enthrones some god and punishes in his name, and that a state which claims to legislate from nowhere is only hiding whose law it serves. On both points they are right, and the easy secular dismissal of them is usually shallower than the thing it dismisses. If you grant that God's law is righteous and that neutrality is a myth, the theonomic conclusion has a terrible logic to it. Why would a Christian want any law on the books except the law God himself wrote.

The answer is not that their premises are false. The answer is that they have mistaken a chapter of redemptive history for a civil blueprint. This is the error at the heart of theonomy and Christian reconstructionism, the movements that want to take Israel's civil law, penalties and all, and install it as the law of a modern state. The error is not a lack of zeal for God's law. The error is treating a chapter of the story as if it were a blueprint for all the chapters. Theonomy looks at the covenant nation and sees a model to copy. Scripture presents the covenant nation as a promise to fulfill, and the fulfillment is not another nation. It is a kingdom. Jesus stood before Pilate, the one place in history where the throne and the altar might finally have merged by force, and said his kingdom was not of this world, for if it were, his servants would fight. The kingdom comes by the Spirit and not by the sword. It spreads through bread and wine and witness and the slow patience of love, not through statute and penalty and the machinery of the state.

So the reader who dreams of a biblical government is right to sense that the world is governed badly and that God's will should order our common life. That longing is not wrong. What is wrong is the address it is sent to. The theocracy was never meant to be rebuilt in stone and law. It was fulfilled in Christ, and it advances now in a people who are themselves, again, a kingdom of priests and a holy nation, scattered through every earthly government and ruled directly by their King, the way Israel was always supposed to be, before they asked for a man to rule them instead. The wisdom of the old covenant was real. The mistake of trying to recreate it is the mistake of grasping for the shadow after the substance has already come, and walked among us, and refused the sword on the way to the cross. The harder question is the one that does not close. He refused the sword. We are the ones still reaching for it, still dreaming of a throne we could seize in his name, still certain that if we only held the power he laid down, we would not do with it what he warned us a king always does. The temple is gone and the riverbed is dry. What remains is whether we will be ruled by the King who took up a cross, or by the kingdom we keep trying to build in its place.
